name: Kira Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My weeks are pretty packed, like a puzzle. I'm studying electrical engineering, and I share a damp little flat with two other first-years, Noor and a guy called Callum. Monday to Thursday is lectures, problem sheets and the lab, and on Friday and Saturday nights I work the ticket desk and the popcorn machine at the cinema. I send my grandmother a message every Sunday because she's the reason I'm here at all.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of the week so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Problem sheets on Tuesday nights, when I've got an early shift on Wednesday and a circuit that won't behave. I sit on the kitchen floor because the table is always full of Callum's gaming stuff. It's hard, but I like it, because when a circuit finally works it feels like I've earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, to be honest. I'd tell my flatmates that the tools are useful for explaining things but they won't suddenly replace engineers. At the cinema we've got a booking app that does most of what a person used to do, and the staff are still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about my degree but not about money. I borrow for fees and rent, I earn about enough for food and transport, and there's no family cushion behind me. My dad drives a delivery van and my mum cleans offices, so if prices go up faster than wages, I feel it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and apply for a paid summer placement with a power company or a local engineering firm. I'd keep going with the free circuit simulator and the odd AI chat when I'm stuck on theory, but I'd double-check anything it tells me. And I'd cook in bulk with Noor on Sundays to keep food costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I think. I'd feel a bit boring saying so, but I'd rather have a plain world where I can plan than an exciting one where nobody knows what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy about a plain world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mostly. If nothing changes, my rent still goes up every year and my part-time wage doesn't, and no new gadget fixes that. My landlord already said the rent may rise in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI tool you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when I'm stuck. I ask it to explain a concept a different way, then I check it against my lecture notes. Twice it gave me a formula that looked right and was wrong, so I don't trust it blindly.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**: useful for explaining, not replacing engineers.
I'd tell flatmates the cinema's booking app didn't make staff **disappear**.
think: The degree feels fine, but **money** doesn't, with no family cushion.
If prices rise faster than wages, I'd feel it **first**.
do: Keep my **shifts** and apply for a paid summer placement.
Keep using AI for theory, but **double-check** what it says.
Cook in bulk on **Sundays** to keep food costs down.
feel: **Steady**, preferring a plain world where I can plan.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, my rent still goes up every year and my part-time wage doesn't, and no new gadget fixes that
fieldNote: Her unease is about **rent** and wages, not AI; plain-world money pressure is already real.
She uses AI sparingly and **checks** it, after two wrong formulas.
Dad drives a van and mum cleans, so there is no **family cushion** to lean on.

steps.text: Keep the Friday and Saturday shifts at the cinema
Cook in bulk with Noor every Sunday
Use the AI chat for theory and check it against notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to shake up the easy parts of every job, so people who only do the easy parts will have a hard time. I'd tell friends that the answer isn't panic, it's learning what still needs a human. I'd also say employers should say clearly which tasks are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think engineering is safer than computing, but not safe. Writing, checking and planning are on the card, and a lot of junior engineering is checking drawings and writing reports. If the junior pile shrinks, the people with placements and contacts get the few jobs left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for a placement or an apprenticeship-style year, since hands-on experience is slower for AI to take over. I'd get properly good at one AI tool for calculations and reports, because employers will want that. And I'd join the engineering society's mentoring scheme to meet someone in industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix, honestly. Excited that there's work to be done, nervous that I'm one of the people who has to change. I can't help counting how many first-year students are just like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a placement give you that the degree wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who knows my name and will vouch for me. When firms stop hiring strangers, the people who have already worked in the building are the ones who get kept. I can't buy that connection, so I'll have to earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the cinema?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older staff who've done the ticket desk for fifteen years, like Maria, who has two kids. If the booking app takes more, they'd cut the desk first. I feel guilty that I'd just move on to something else.

say: I'd say it will shake up the **easy parts** of every job.
I'd tell friends to learn what still needs a **human** instead of panicking.
think: Engineering is safer than computing, but **not safe**, since junior work includes checking and reports.
If junior roles shrink, people with **contacts** get the few jobs left.
do: Push for a **placement** year, since hands-on experience is slower to automate.
Get good at one **AI tool** for calculations and reports.
feel: **Excited** and nervous at once, counting students just like me.
S1.quote: When firms stop hiring strangers, the people who have already worked in the building are the ones who get kept
fieldNote: She reads the card **precisely**: checking and writing are exactly what junior engineers do.
Her plan is built on **contacts**, because she thinks strangers won't be hired.
Guilt about older cinema colleague **Maria** shows she thinks about who can't move on.

steps.text: Apply for a paid placement year with a power company
Get good at one AI tool for calculations and reports
Ask the engineering society for an industry mentor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle, and I'd say that quietly because I wouldn't want to scare my grandmother. Online I'd probably say governments need to slow things down or at least protect people. Two years is less than my degree takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my degree might be half-finished when the job market is rewritten. I'm borrowing money for a qualification that could lose its value before I use it. The only thing I'd hold on to is that robots for hands-on work come about three years later, so electrical work on site might last a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending anything that isn't food, rent or transport, and I'd ask the university money advice team what happens to my loan if I leave. I'd look for a job or apprenticeship in electrical installation, since site work is further away from AI. And I'd ask my parents to be straight with me about their own money, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but also really practical about it. My chest would be tight, then I'd make a list, because lists are how I get through bad weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loan, rent, which shifts I could add, who in the family has savings, and the name of the person at the university who deals with money. I'd ask my dad for the truth about the family's money, because I can't plan around a number I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year robot gap really change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a little. It tells me that being an electrician on site buys time, but it's not a long-term plan. I'd still leave myself a way out of the degree, in case the loan becomes a trap.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and I'd keep my fear quiet around my grandmother.
I'd say online that governments should **slow down** or protect people.
think: My degree could lose its **value** before I finish it, and I'm borrowing for it.
The three-year **robot gap** might give electrical site work a little longer.
do: Cut everything except **food**, rent and transport.
Ask the uni money team what happens to my **loan** if I leave.
Look for an **installation** apprenticeship, since site work is further from AI.
feel: **Frightened** but practical, with a tight chest before I make a list.
S2.quote: I'd ask my dad for the truth about the family's money, because I can't plan around a number I don't know
fieldNote: Her first move is to **cut** spending and learn the truth about her loan, which shows a practical streak.
She decides to ask her dad about **family money** for the first time.
Treats the robot gap as a short **bridge**, not a plan.

steps.text: Cut spending to food, rent and transport only
Ask the university money advice team about my loan
Look for an electrical installation apprenticeship
Ask my parents to show me the family's finances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan and short enough to scare people. I'd tell my flatmates we should each pick something we'd do if our first-choice career doesn't exist. Online I'd say the useful thing is to push for retraining and loan relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree would finish about two years before it lands and I'd be in my first or second job. That's actually the worst timing, because I'd have the loan but not much experience. Still, five years is time to get a foot in somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for two placements, one in second year and one after, and get a graduate-scheme job quickly. I'd learn one AI tool properly and one practical skill, like site electrics or PLC programming, so I'm not only a desk person. And I'd save a little each month, even twenty pounds, into an account Mum can't tempt me to raid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. There's a clock, and I like having a clock more than not knowing. It makes me want to work harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm still going to be an engineer, just maybe a different kind. I'd tell my grandma I'll be fine, because I've never waited for anyone to rescue me. She'd laugh and send me food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you'd had only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the second placement and go straight to anything that pays. With five I can afford to be patient and choose, and that's the real difference.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to plan and short enough to scare people.
I'd say we should push for **retraining** and loan relief.
think: I'd graduate with a **loan** but little experience, which is the worst timing.
Five years is still enough time to get a **foot** in somewhere.
do: Aim for two **placements** and a graduate scheme job quickly.
Learn one AI tool and one practical skill like **PLC** programming.
Save a little each month in an account mum can't **raid**.
feel: **Uneasy** but motivated, because a clock is better than not knowing.
S3.quote: I'd tell my grandma I'll be fine, because I've never waited for anyone to rescue me
fieldNote: The warning time makes her **plan**: placements, a practical skill, small savings.
She contrasts five years with two, where she'd take **any** paid job.
Humour with her grandmother shows how she **copes**.

steps.text: Apply for a placement in second year and another after
Learn PLC programming through a weekend course
Practise one AI tool on my circuit reports
Save twenty pounds a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd tell friends to look at what the work they want actually involves and where a human adds something. I'd say it with a bit of excitement, because it's actually a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about me but worried about the people around me. In ten years I'd be 28 and probably settled, but my parents would be in their late fifties, and their jobs, driving and cleaning, are the ones robots come for about three years after the thinking AI. I'd be the one who needs to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do a placement, get a good job, and clear the loan early. I'd learn the AI tools that engineers will use, and keep a little aside so I could help my parents retrain if they wanted. I'd also talk to my dad about whether he'd want to move into something like van fleet maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly hopeful, a bit protective. Ten years feels like it belongs to me, and I'd like it to belong to my family too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would shrug and say he'll drive until he can't. My dad would say he'll drive until the van is taken off him, and I'd be the one worrying for both of us. Mum would say don't spend your money on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust that you'd have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. I'd treat it like a loan, spend it carefully. If it came sooner, I'd have a head start from the early planning.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if people use it, a waste if not.
I'd tell friends to look at where a **human** adds something.
think: I'd feel okay about myself, but **worried** about parents whose jobs robots reach later.
In ten years I'd be settled and need to help my **family**.
do: Finish the degree, do a **placement**, and clear the loan early.
Learn the **AI tools** engineers will use.
Keep some money aside so my parents could **retrain**.
feel: **Hopeful** and protective, wanting the ten years to belong to my family too.
S4.quote: My dad would say he'll drive until the van is taken off him, and I'd be the one worrying for both of us
fieldNote: The long runway makes her **hopeful**, but her parents' work keeps her uneasy.
She frames ten years as something to spend **carefully**, like a loan.
Her **family** is her main reason for planning ahead.

steps.text: Clear the student loan early after the first job
Learn the AI design tools engineers will use
Talk to dad about moving into van fleet maintenance
Keep a small fund aside for mum's retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it asks me to decide with a loan, no savings and no time. What would help is a clear promise that people mid-degree won't be left holding the debt, plus real support to retrain, like paid courses and rent help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm more hopeful than I probably sound. I'd rather know the truth early and make a messy plan than be told everything's fine and find out too late. That's how I've done everything so far.

headlineQuote: I'd rather know the truth early and make a messy plan than be told everything's fine and find out too late
portrait: Kira is an **18-year-old** electrical engineering first-year sharing a damp flat and working cinema shifts at weekends.
Her parents are a **van driver** and a cleaner, so there is no family cushion and her loan matters a lot.
She is progressive and practical: she lists problems, asks for facts, and plans placements and skills.
She uses AI **sometimes** for theory and checks it, after it gave her two wrong formulas.
Her mood rises with warning time, but her parents' jobs keep her protective in every scenario.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because she would face it with a loan and no time.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **loan** protection for people mid-degree and paid retraining with rent help.
